clinicalPearls: The hallmark of the condition is bilateral vestibular schwannomas, which typically present with progressive sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance in adolescence or early adulthood
It is a distinct disorder from neurofibromatosis type 1: NF2 is dominated by schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas rather than the neurofibromas, café-au-lait macules, and Lisch nodules of NF1
Additional tumours include cranial and spinal meningiomas, spinal and peripheral nerve schwannomas, and intramedullary or cauda equina ependymomas
A characteristic ophthalmological clue is juvenile posterior subcapsular or cortical cataract, which may predate tumour diagnosis

The disorder is caused by loss-of-function variants in the NF2 tumour suppressor gene, which encodes merlin (schwannomin); it is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern but a large proportion of cases are de novo and mosaicism is common
Management is delivered through specialist multidisciplinary teams, using serial MRI surveillance of the brain and spine and audiological monitoring

Treatment prioritises hearing preservation; the anti-VEGF agent bevacizumab can shrink vestibular schwannomas and improve hearing in selected cases, alongside microsurgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, and auditory implantation
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder results from inactivating germline variants in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, which encodes merlin (also called schwannomin), a cytoskeletal linker protein that normally suppresses cell proliferation by regulating contact inhibition and several growth-signalling pathways. Loss of functional merlin, following a second somatic hit in Schwann cells, meningeal cells, and ependymal cells, removes this brake and predisposes to multiple nervous-system tumours. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance, though many patients harbour de novo variants and somatic mosaicism, which influences severity and the recurrence risk offered during counselling.
additionalDifferentials: Von Hippel-Lindau disease (other inherited tumour predisposition)
Meningioma predisposition from prior cranial irradiation
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain (including internal auditory meati) and whole spine
Molecular genetic testing of the NF2 gene, with tumour testing where mosaicism is suspected
Pure-tone audiometry and speech discrimination testing with serial monitoring
Brainstem auditory evoked responses to assess auditory pathway function
Ophthalmological examination for juvenile cataract and retinal lesions
Baseline neurological and dermatological assessment for schwannomas and skin tumours
redFlags: Rapidly progressive hearing loss or brainstem compression from an enlarging vestibular schwannoma
New or worsening myelopathy or radiculopathy from spinal tumours
Raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus from large posterior fossa lesions
Facial nerve dysfunction or lower cranial nerve palsies indicating local tumour progression
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and progressive, with morbidity driven by cumulative tumour burden, hearing loss, and the risks of surgery near critical neural structures. Early diagnosis, expert multidisciplinary surveillance, and hearing-preservation strategies have improved outcomes, but the disorder shortens life expectancy on average and disease is generally more aggressive when it presents in childhood.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the disorder as NF1 and expecting neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules rather than schwannomas and meningiomas
Treating a young person's vestibular schwannoma as sporadic and failing to image the contralateral side and spine
Overlooking mosaicism, which can give falsely reassuring blood genetic testing and complicate counselling
Delaying referral to a specialist centre, where hearing-preservation and multidisciplinary planning materially affect outcome
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
management: Deliver care through a specialist multidisciplinary team with serial contrast-enhanced MRI surveillance of the brain and whole spine and regular audiological monitoring
Manage vestibular schwannomas with a hearing-preservation approach, choosing between observation, microsurgery and stereotactic radiosurgery according to tumour growth and hearing
Use bevacizumab to reduce vestibular schwannoma volume and stabilise or improve hearing in progressive disease
Treat meningiomas and ependymomas with surgery or radiosurgery as dictated by symptoms and growth
Support hearing and communication with hearing aids, and offer auditory brainstem or cochlear implantation when hearing is lost
Provide ophthalmological review for juvenile cataract and monitor for other nervous-system tumours
Offer genetic counselling, molecular testing and family screening, accounting for the high rate of de novo variants and mosaicism
